Religion Corner - Main Mother’s Day 2025 By Pastor Jim Hopkins I was visiting one of our older members this past week and she asked me what I was going to preach about today. I answered, “Well, it is going to be Mother’s Day so I imagine that I will extol mothers.” She replied, “As well you should!” Beyond following her exhortation and extolling mothers in a general way, and while recognizing that mother is a role and title that transcends biology, I want to thank each mother, grandmother and great-grandmother among us for the way you continue the work of Tabitha, known in Greek as Dorcas, from Joppa in ancient Israel. We read her story in Acts 9:26-43. That text describes Tabitha as a disciple, the only time the feminine form of disciple is used in the New Testament. It tells us she was “devoted to good works and acts of charity” and it informs us that she became ill and died. The other members of the Christ community in Joppa, having prepared her body in the traditional way, sent two of their number to Peter, who was in a nearby village, requesting him to come to Joppa at once. Peter came with them and they took him to the upstairs room where Tabitha’s body lay. In that room there was a wake going on. There were tears, prayers, and stories. The beautiful clothing that she renowned for making was on display. Clearly, Tabitha was beloved. Clearly, her community was going to miss her greatly. Then Peter did something unexpected. He asked everyone to leave the room. When they were gone he knelt down and prayed. Turning to her body he said, loudly or quietly we do not know, “Tabitha, get up.” What happened next was even more unexpected. The text reads, “Then she opened her eyes and seeing Peter, she sat up. He gave her his hand and helped her up. Then calling the saints and widows, he showed her to be alive.” Of course Tabitha’s resurrection was an occasion for great rejoicing and the cause of many becoming followers of Jesus. It was also something much more. articles.text: Piedmont’s Public Works department recently finished some vegetation management work to reduce fire risk near Moraga Canyon. The work began on April 22 and finished last week. The work was performed uphill behind the City’s Corporation Yard to remove shrubs and tree branch vegetation less than six feet in height. This type of vegetation, known sometimes as “ladder fuels,” can behave as a ladder for fires to reach treetops in the event of a wildfire. Workers clear away potential fire hazards on the hill overlooking Piedmont’s Corporation Yard. Public Works vehicles carry out bunches of dried branches from the hilltop. A worker with a chainsaw removes a low-hanging tree. If a “ladder fuel” like this catches fire, it could spread to higher tree branches and accelerate a wildfire. Removal of these ladder fuels is recommended by the Piedmont Fire Department as a best practice. With the Corporation Yard hillside so steep, this work can be dangerous and complex, but can also make a big impact in terms of fire protection. This is the second year Public Works has performed this particular type of weed cutting in the area, continuing a project that began in 2024 to reduce fire fuel loads on City property in Moraga Canyon. Last year, Public Works focused their efforts on the area on the east side of the hill because of its proximity to several homes on Maxwelton Road, Echo Lane, and Abbott Way. In the event of a wildfire, the vegetation removal would provide a critical buffer for homes on the hill. The goats will make their annual visit to the area soon to reduce fire risk by dining on the grasses. This work clears the way for the grass clearing to be even more effective this year, removing obstacles between the goats and their dinner. “Continuing to perform fuel load reduction/fire mitigation work is an essential tool for staff to help prepare the City and community for the fire season,” said Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales.

articles.text: Build It, Launch It, Make It! 11th Annual Maker Faire Returns Sunday The 11th annual Piedmont School Maker Faire returns to the Piedmont High School campus this Sunday, May 18, 11:00 a.m. - 3:00 p.m. Come celebrate K-12 Science, Technology, Engineering, Arts & Math (S.T.E.A.M.) education for the Piedmont community and beyond. Organized by Piedmont Makers, this beloved event will showcase more than 80 projects featuring the S.T.E.A.M. creativity, passion, and effort of makers in our community. Many of these projects are created by Piedmont students. From robotics and rocketry to handcrafted art and engineering marvels, the Faire celebrates the power of STEAM through creativity, collaboration, and invention. This isn’t just a showcase— it’s an experience. Families and curious minds of all ages can dive into dozens of hands-on activities, from returning fan favorites like Maker River, Air Rockets, and the Nerdy Derby to exciting new experiences like Mini Golf Links, fresh apple juice pressing, and even making your own paintbrushes and jewelry. For the sustainably minded, there are opportunities to bring your old electronics to be repaired and swap STEAM toys. Musical guests are the Piedmont High School Jazz Combo, Pied mont Middle School Orchestra groups, and Camino’s Jazz. Food will also be available at the Faire, including delicious lunch options from Chef Robert Dorsey and Boba Tea from Tea on Piedmont. Free tickets are available at www.piedmontmakers.org. articles.text: Piedmont botanical artist Bonnie Bonner, also known as Joanne Palamountain, will demonstrate how to create Bug Hotels for pollinators using renewable, found materials during the 2025 Piedmont School Maker Faire. The Bug Hotels — along with hundreds of other STEAM projects and demonstrations — will be open to the public on the Piedmont High School campus Sunday, May 18, from 11:00 a.m. to 3:00 p.m. Bug Hotels are hanging garden art that provide protection for beneficial insects. Like organic litter found naturally on the forest floor, reclaimed plant matter offers pollinators and other helpful insects a place to feed, rest, propagate and hide from predators. Essential to our ecosystem, native wasps, beetles, lacewings and ladybugs are among the tenants that take up residence in the hidden hollows and tunnels. Bug hotels are ready to hang indoors or outside. These sustainable shelters foster habitats that support biodiversity and remind the public that insects need our help. They also highlight the simple beauty of nature. You can find more than 50 of Bonnie’s Bug Hotels hanging in Piedmont backyard gardens and front porticoes. View more on her website gallery at: BonniesBotanicalArt.com/bug-hotels Bonnie Bonner makes one-of-kind insect habitats as hanging garden art from seed pods and other recycled plant matter.

articles.text: Sixty-two students, mentors, and family members travelled to Houston in April for the FIRST World Championship. This April, 50,000 people and 600 teams from 18 countries converged on Houston for the FIRST World Championship in robotics. During the four-day competition, Highlander Robotics — Team 8033 — earned the Engineering Excellence Award for their robot, “Kelpie.” The team faced a tough qualification round in the 75-team Johnson Division, with three close matches ending in narrow losses (159–160, 225–221, 180–181). Despite finishing 43rd in qualifications with a 3–7 record, they were selected 14th overall in the playoff draft by the fifth-seeded alliance. The team ultimately finished fifth in the double-elimination playoff bracket. In judged awards, the Highlanders received the “Excellence in Engineering” honor, which recognizes a professional approach to the design process and consistent high-performance operation. With the competition season concluded, Highlander Robotics now ranks in the top 3% of all teams worldwide. Next up for the team is an open house and recruiting session during the Piedmont School Maker Faire. On May 18, the team will open the doors of the Mary G. Ross Engineering Lab at 2 p.m. to prospective students, parents and community members. The event offers a chance to tour the lab, meet the dedicated mentors and students behind the award-winning team, and learn how to get involved. articles.text: Shelby, Long qualify in 4 events; Kim wins 100 hurdles Piedmont High’s track and field team had a tremendous showing at the 2025 Western .Alameda County Conference Championship meet on Wednesday and Friday, May 7-9. With top-six finishes, Piedmont officially qualified in 24 events for the North Coast Section Bayshore Area Championship at Vallejo HS on Saturday, May 17. The Highlanders won four league titles: Nia Kim in the 100 hurdles, Andrea Martin in the shot put, Sebastien Swain in the 1600, and the boys’ relay team of Maddox Ma, Eric Venner, Ben Gerber, and Rehan Mumtaz in the 4x400. Kim, a first-year varsity member, won her event in 15.62 seconds in a field of 20 hurdlers. She also placed second of 15 in the high jump with a height of five feet even. Kim ran the first leg in the 4x100 relay team with Ella Yasar, Kyla Williams, and Claire Aubrecht, which placed second of 10 teams in 49.76. She also ran the first leg in the 4x400. The team with Aubrecht, Daniela Lucaccini, and Yasar finished second of 10 in a time of 4:07.99. Nia, a senior, has been a breakthrough for the track and field team in her first-year as a varsity athlete. She elected to join the squad after previously competing in gymnastics. “I did gymnastics for a long time before this. I’ve always been pretty fast, so when I knew I was done with gymnastics, I wanted to try out. I honestly thought I would just do sprints, I didn’t expect to do hurdles or relays,” Kim said. She found her athleticism from gymnastics translated well to the track. Now nearing the end of her only year competing at the high school level, Kim is a league champion. “The first time I tried hurdles, it was just for fun because my friends were trying it. My first one didn’t go very well, but after that, I thought I could get it Photo by Becky Spies Nia Kim. a first-year varsity athlete won the league title in the 100- meter hurdles. Staff photos Sebastien Swain won the 1600 meters and just missed winning the 800. down. Coach P saw it and told me to keep working at it. It’s really exciting to win. First of all, I never thought I’d be doing hurdles, so to be good at them and be able to have great coaches, it’s amazing,” Kim said. Martin has been another breakthrough athlete. A basketball star as a freshman, she broke her own school record in the shot with a distance of 34 feet, 1.5 inches to take firstplace out of 36 athletes. She also placed fourth in the high jump at 4 feet, 10 inches. Distance runner Swain, a sophomore, qualified in two events, winning the 1600 with a time of 4:21.01 in a field of 54 runners. He also came narrowly close to winning the 800, finishing second of 47 in 1:57.33, falling to Bishop O’Dowd’s James Prater by .08 of a second. The boys’ 4x400 relay team of Ma, Venner, Gerber, and Mumtaz finished in 3:31.83 against nine other teams. They beat O’Dowd for second place by .23 of a second. Piedmont senior Sam Shelby had a big day, qualifying in four different events. He finished fifth of 50 in the 100-meter sprint in 11.28 seconds, was third of 41 in the 200 in 22.26, and was second of 45 runners in the 400 in 49.89. He ran the second leg of the 4x100 relay team with Mumtaz, Ma, and Venner, which placed second of 10 in 42.88. His times in the 200 and 400 marked personal records. His time of 22.26 in the 200 broke Kyle Dalton’s 2013 school record of 22.36. He is now .02 of a second behind Kevin Hogan’s school record set 66 years ago in the 220-yard event of 22.24. “I’ve had that number on my wall all season. It’s a big deal for me personally; just to know I accomplished that goal is a huge weight off my shoulders. It was a big moment for me,” Shelby said. Shelby missed most of his junior track season due to an injury. With that, he circled 2025 as his year to produce. “Last season was definitely not what I wanted it to be. articles.text: Piedmont High junior Lucas Smolko continued his strong season at the Division 2 North Coast Section Individual Tournament on Friday and Saturday, May 9-10 at Vintage High School in Napa. He reached the singles championship match before losing in three sets to Head Royce’s Dylan Donovan, 5-7, 6-1, 6-3. Smolko was the bracket’s No. 2 seed, while Donovan was No. 1. articles.text: Highlanders reach first NCS Semifinals since 2019 Piedmont’s No. 6 seeded girls’ lacrosse team was victorious in the first two rounds of the Division 2 North Coast Section playoffs over the past week. They defeated No. 11 Cardinal Newman 16-3 at Witter Field in the opening round on Tuesday, May 6 before upsetting No. 3 Lick-Wilmerding 5-4 at the Beach Chalet Fields in San Francisco on Thursday, May 8. The pair of wins means Piedmont will play in its first NCS Semifinals since 2019, when they won the NCS Div. 2 title. The Highlanders played rival Bishop O’Dowd in Oakland for the semifinals on Tuesday, May 13. Results were not complete by press time. To reach the semifinals is a testament to their grit and tenacity with a squad that contrasts to the championship winning team from six years ago. The 2019 team was the school’s best of all time. They finished 20-2 with a roster that included a number of players who went on to play colPeyton Watson scored three goals against Lick-Wilmerding and eight against Cardinal Newman. Chloe Graham scored two goals against Lick-Wilmerding and four in the game with Cardinal Newman. Staff Photos Piedmont’s No. 6 seeded girls’ lacrosse team upset No. 3 LickWilmerding to reach its first NCS Semifinals since 2019. legiately: Elie Cole, Zoe Torok, Widdy Tevis, Maria Del Rosario Chan, and all-time assist leader Sadie Tschider. This year, Piedmont is 10-9 overall and finished third in the league tournament. The WACC has shown its quality with Berkeley, O’Dowd, and Piedmont all reaching the NCS semifinals. “They willed every skill set out of themselves to get here. That 2019 team was very different; this team is filled with hard workers, it was about doing all the little things. articles.text: When a high school pitcher is dealing his best quality all season, it’s sometimes difficult to get out from under. That was the case in Monday, May 12’s Western Alameda County Conference Semifinals at Humphries Diamond, where No. 2 seeded Piedmont lost 6-0 to No. 3 Encinal, whose pitcher Kyle Cooke nearly threw a perfect game with no hits allowed, 10 strikeouts, and one walk. “He pitched a great game. That’s the third time we’ve seen him this year and he’s beaten us twice. He was really on his game mixing up his pitches. We were definitely off of our timing and he deserves the credit. He’s a really quality pitcher,” coach Eric Olson said. The loss is a testament to Staff Photos Piedmont’s baseball team looks ahead to the North Coast Section tournament. Piedmont split games with Encinal, Berkeley, Bishop O’Dowd, and regular season champs Castro Valley. Piedmont similarly walked into last year’s WACC Tournament with the top seed, but lost to Alameda in the semifinals. Despite the loss, the Highlanders look to recapture 2024’s magic when they reached the Division 4 North Coast Section Championship game and the D4 CIF NorCal title game. “We went on a run last year. It’s just about playing the best baseball at the right time,” Olson added. “It’s not always the best team who wins, it’s the team that plays the best to win. articles.text: 8th graders Travers Kemp (8th) and Dylan Wallway were joined by sixth grader Elijah Simon to run the 4x400 relay at the league track meet at King Middle School on May 8. It was the last event of the night, and there were not enough runners for PMS to field an 8th grade boys team, so Kemp and Wallway (who had just finished running the 200 and mile, respectively), recruited Simon, a 6th grader who had finished his 200 not long before. He happily stepped up and helped Piedmont place 2nd in the event. “Despite the late hour, the empty stands, and their exhaustion after five hours of competition, they had a great race. All the runners gave everything they had left in the tank,” said coach MInori Tsuge. Even with only three racers (Travers ran both the first and last legs), the boys finished in 2nd place for the 8th grade teams, and 3rd out of 12 teams overall. “The support they gave to each other is what we are looking for in coaching the students. It is considered Northern California’s premier mixed-terrain cycling competition. The series stretches from January 26 to May 10 and is known for its challenging blend of gravel, pavement, and dirt courses to test riders across multiple events. The races take place in Northern California, in Ukiah, Maxwell, Sonoma County, and Duncan Mills, CA on public roads, private trails, and through public parks. The Grasshopper Adventure Series, now in its 28th year, is celebrated for pushing cyclists through some of Northern California’s most demanding terrains. Each event offers a unique course, combining various surfaces to challenge participants’ versatility and endurance. Schuetz secured 46 points Jasper Schuetz was fifth of 32 riders at Stafford Lake. He already clinched the title by his last race on May 10th at King Ridge in Duncan Mills, which was a distance of 91 miles with 9,116 feet of elevation gain. The ride featured steep climbs, technical descents, winding roads, and a coastal ride from Bodega Bay to Timber Cove. This combination of results placed him at the top of the Junior U19 Male category. The workshop is open to visitors of all levels of photographic experience. Citret, a San Francisco native, began photographing in 1968 and in the 1980’s produced a large body of work titled “Unnatural Wonders,” his personal survey of architecture in national parks. articles.text: The San Francisco Opera orchestra will perform a free concert at historic Saint Joseph’s Arts Society in San Francisco on Saturday, May 17. Advanced registration is required. The afternoon performance, entitled SoundCheck, features music from The Young Person’s Guide to the Orchestra, Benjamin Britten’s classic introduction to the instruments, sounds and personalities of the orchestra. Orchestra musicians will also perform Henry Purcell’s original theme from the play Abdelazer, which inspired Britten’s famous composition, and Richard Wagner’s Siegfried Idyll. San Francisco Opera Music Director Eun Sun Kim will conduct the full orchestra for this performance, suitable for families and music lovers of all ages. Attendees are encouraged to move about the iconic space to experience the varied sounds of the orchestra from different perspectives. Saint Joseph’s Arts Society, founded by Ken Fulk in 2018, was established to celebrate and promote arts, design and culture in the San Francisco Bay Area. St. Joseph’s Arts Society is located in a revitalized National Historic Landmark former church, providing an intimate setting for the San Francisco Opera’s free concert. SoundCheck begins at 2:30 p.m. at Saint Joseph’s Arts Society at 1401 Howard Street in the SOMA neighborhood of San Francisco. Doors open at 1:30 p.m. and attendees may purchase drinks at a cash-only bar. Limited seating will be available on a first-come, first-served basis. articles.text: American Conservatory Theater (A.C.T.) presents the world premiere of hip-hop musical Co-Founders at Strand Theater in San Francisco Thursday, May 29. The play runs through Sunday, July 6. Directed by Jamil Jude, the play follows an underrated young Oakland coder named Esata who “hacks” her way into a competitive startup accelerator in San Francisco, the world’s tech mecca. As Esata and her loved ones get priced out by Silicon Valley billionaires, Esata forms an unlikely partnership with a prep-school dropout in a field where the privileged few make millions while others struggle to survive. “This is a musical love letter for the community… [from] the Valley to Vallejo,” said A.C.T. Artistic Director Pam MacKinnon. “I am thrilled that A.C.T. will premiere this Bay story. Strand Theater is sure to be the place this Spring to feel big joy with this big local can-do story born of necessity and drive, creativity and passion. Created by local playwrights and artists RyanNicole Austin, Beau Lewis, and Adesha Adefela, Co-Founders features a catchy Photo by Michaela Schulz Co-Founders creative team Beau Lewis, Adesha Adefela, and RyanNicole Austin score that draws inspiration from the Bay Area’s hip-hop scene, as well as soul, gospel, funk, jazz, R&B, and more. “I’m thrilled to launch Co-Founders right here in the Bay, my home and heart,” Austin said. “This show is an ode to our region, celebrating a spirit of innovation so vibrant, resilient, and determinant it blooms through concrete like dandelions. Co-Founders is both a loving critique and an invitation for today’s visionaries to reflect deeply on the future they’re building.” The cast of Co-Founders includes Adefela and Austin, as well as Austin Dean Ashford, Rolanda D. Bell, Jordan Covington, B. DeVeaux, Aneesa Folds, Roe Hartrampf, Keith Pinto, Deanalís Arocho Resto, Tommy Soulati Shepherd, and Ryan Torres. Post-show discussions with the creative team are held on June 17 and 22, and July 2. A revamped pre- and post-show party celebrating LGBTQ+ pride within the theater community will be held June 18 before and following the 7:30 p.m. performance. To purchase tickets, call the box office at 415-749-2228 or visit www.act-sf.org/cofounders to purchase online.

articles.text: The 42nd San Francisco Jazz Festival, an annual three-week music festival produced by nonprofit organization SFJAZZ, kicks off on Friday, June 13 at the Miner Auditorium. articles.text: Piedmont resident Joel Sidney performed on guitar with the Spectrum Bluegrass Band to a near capacity audience for the Light Up the Blues concert on April 26 at the 5,900-seat Los Angeles Greek Theatre. Joel is a graduate of Piedmont High School and received a B.A. degree from the University of California in Berkeley. Other band members included Joy Louise Williams (guitar), John Frizzell (mandolin), Jesse Katz (bass) and Max Schwartz (banjo). The band played three songs including two bluegrass standards, “On and On” and “Blue Moon of Kentucky” and one song composed by Williiams, “Majestic Breed.” The 4-hour concert was headlined by performances from the legendary Stephen Stills and Neil Young as well as other famous artists including Billy Idol, Cat Power, Linda Perry, Chris Stills, Nathaniel Rateliff, and Rufus Wainwright. The Light Up the Blues concert was sponsored by and benefited Autism Speaks (www. autismspeaks.org), a non-profit organization dedicated to creating an inclusive world for all individuals with autism throughout their lifespan. The Spectrum Bluegrass Band was sponsored by the California Bluegrass Association though its new initiative, Spectrum Bluegrass (https://californiabluegrass.org/ spectrum-bluegrass/) which is dedicated to connecting neurodiverse people through bluegrass music. Spectrum Bluegrass is starting with an Autism Chapter with a goal to ease the challenges and amplify the enjoyment of bluegrass for autistic people by creating an active community where they explore new pathways to express themselves and connect. Spectrum Bluegrass Band performed at the Light Up the Blues concert. Band members are Joy Louise Williams (left), Joel Sidney, John Frissell, Jesse Katz, and Max Schwartz San Francisco Bach Choir The very next day, the San Francisco Bach Choir conducted by Magen Solomon presented a concert in First Church Berkeley. First on the program came a Mass written by Marianna Martines (1744-1812). This composition was written when she was only 16 years old. I had never heard of her. A genius like this… and totally unknown. When listening to music it’s often helpful to begin with a clean slate. There was a Mozartian clarity thoroughly embracing the spirit of the classic era. It seems that Marianna Martines was highly respected early on and then became forgotten. If this work is any indication, it will be a pleasure to hear other works by her. The San Francisco Bach choir was directed by Magen Solomon, who also conducted the Jubilate Baroque Orchestra. Solomon’s conducting was gracious, encouraging and intelligent. As a result, the performance was gracious, encouraging and intelligent. Martha Stoddard, the conductor of the Piedmont Chamber Orchestra visited with me for a little while during the intermission. She told me that the PCO will play a concert Saturday afternoon, May 17 at 4:00 p.m. in the Alan Harvey Theater. Diluvian String Quartet A familial responsibility encouraged me to attend the Diluvian string Quartet concert in the Piedmont Center for the Arts that same afternoon. Son Raphael is the violist. They have a new cellist. While listening to any concert, I form my own opinions. At the same time, I listen to what members of the audience say, and I even engage them in conversation, asking for their opinions. Some of the observations were in complete agreement with mine. They observed that the tone of the Diluvian String Quartet is like wine of a rare vintage… mellow and well-balanced.

articles.text: Can there be too much of a good thing? In music, we have the term ma non troppo, which means “but not too much”. I assume this means that musicians have a good amount of equilibrium. What is difficult is making the choice at the banquet table. It is a pleasure to see how child prodigies grow into mature artists. That was the case at Piedmont Piano Company on Friday evening when two of the outstanding young talents from our area presented an exciting concert. Melissa Lam is a cellist of high attainment… snd still a high school student. She was joined by pianist and composer Eric Tran. The concert featured Sonata by Mendelssohn and Rachmaninov. It is hard to imagine better compositions. What we heard was a sublime interpretation. Tran introduced the works with a little bit of levity – and then the two of them played. They did not need to warm up. They were hot from the start. The performance gave me goosebumps. In my notes, I wrote the word “thrilling“ and then added an exclamation point. This was classic Mendelsohn. It encapsulated ardent and playful leprechauns, playful but evil fairies, a love song and bees in the garden. Both the Mendelssohn Sonata, and the Rachmaninoff Sonata have a universality. The performance expressed this nature, causing the listener to be transported to another world. The two young musicians play with the wisdom of the ages. They have a diabolical intensity and make everything look so easy. In my dictionary, that defines “virtuosity”. Pianist Eric Tran and cellist Melissa Lam take their curtain calls after a masterful concert on May 9 at Piedmont Piano Company.
articles.title: Ma non troppo

This was classic Mendelsohn. It encapsulated ardent and playful leprechauns, playful but evil fairies, a love song and bees in the garden. Both the Mendelssohn Sonata, and the Rachmaninoff Sonata have a universality. The performance expressed this nature, causing the listener to be transported to another world. The two young musicians play with the wisdom of the ages. They have a diabolical intensity and make everything look so easy. In my dictionary, that defines “virtuosity”. Spectrum Bluegrass Band performed at the Light Up the Blues concert. Band members are Joy Louise Williams (left), Joel Sidney, John Frissell, Jesse Katz, and Max Schwartz San Francisco Bach Choir The Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet The very next day, the San Francisco Bach Choir conducted by Magen Solomon presented a concert in First Church Berkeley. First on the program came a Mass written by Marianna Martines (1744-1812). This composition was written when she was only 16 years old. I had never heard of her. A genius like this… and totally unknown. When listening to music it’s often helpful to begin with a clean slate. There was a Mozartian clarity thoroughly embracing the spirit of the classic era. It seems that Marianna Martines was highly respected early on and then became forgotten. If this work is any indication, it will be a pleasure to hear other works by her. The San Francisco Bach choir was directed by Magen Solomon, who also conducted the Jubilate Baroque Orchestra. Solomon’s conducting was gracious, encouraging and intelligent. As a result, the performance was gracious, encouraging and intelligent. Martha Stoddard, the conductor of the Piedmont Chamber Orchestra visited with me for a little while during the intermission. She told me that the PCO will play a concert Saturday afternoon, May 17 at 4:00 p.m. in the Alan Harvey Theater. Diluvian String Quartet A familial responsibility encouraged me to attend the Diluvian string Quartet concert in the Piedmont Center for the Arts that same afternoon. Son Raphael is the violist. They have a new cellist. While listening to any concert, I form my own opinions. At the same time, I listen to what members of the audience say, and I even engage them in conversation, asking for their opinions. Some of the observations were in complete agreement with mine. They observed that the tone of the Diluvian String Quartet is like wine of a rare vintage… mellow and well-balanced. articles.text: The San Francisco Mandolin Octet will perform a concert at Piedmont Center for the Arts on Saturday, May 24. The theme: “Originals: Music Made for Mandolins.” According to Achille Bocus, music director and concert soloist, “the concert will feature music specifically written to highlight the mandolin’s shimmering, expressive sound. It will be an afternoon of original music made specifically for mandolins, with no adaptations and no transcriptions, just authentic compositions that showcase mandolins in their purest form.” At the heart of the program are works by Raffaele Calace, one of the most brilliant and virtuosic mandolin composers of all time. His compositions, full of drama, passion, and astonishing technique, reveal the mandolin’s exceptional capacity for classical expression and virtuosity. Alongside Calace, the octet will showcase other pieces created for small mandolin ensembles with works that highlight the instrument’s unique, sparkling sound and demonstrate the depth of its classical repertoire. It’s an opportunity to hear musical treasures rarely heard in concert halls, and promises to be a distinctive musical experience. The San Francisco Mandolin Octet is an offshoot of the larger San Francisco Mandolin Orchestra, which has performed to appreciative audiences in Piedmont since 2017. The ensemble plays a combination of classical orchestral pieces transcribed for mandolins, mandolas, and guitars, as well as a selection of more popular and contemporary pieces. The family-friendly concert will begin at 4:00 p.m. on Saturday, May 24. Admission is $25 general in advance, and $30 cash/ check at the door. Tickets may be purchased at https://www.brownpapertickets.com/e/6648585

articles.text: Benicia Chamber Players presents the season finale of its 2024–2025 series on May 24 at 7:30 p.m. at the Piedmont Center for the Arts with a program of visionary and virtuosic string ensemble works. The program includes Arnold Schoenberg’s Verklärte Nacht, Richard Strauss’ Capriccio, and Grażyna Bacewicz’s Concerto for String Orchestra (1948). Schoenberg’s late-Romantic tone poem vividly brings Richard Dehmel’s haunting verse to life, exploring despair, forgiveness, and redemption through love. Strauss’ Capriccio, subtitled “A Conversation Piece for Music,” poses the timeless question: which holds greater power—words or music? Composed during World War II, it offers a poignant, lyrical escape. Bacewicz’s vibrant concerto, one of her masterpieces, fuses neoclassical clarity with modern intensity, marked by propulsive rhythms, haunting melodies, and a fiercely original voice that defies easy classification. This concert is free for students. Musicians: Maya Cohon, violin; Heeguen Song, violin; Nao Kubota, viola; Dmitri Yevstifeev, viola; Brady Anderson, cello; Evan Kahn, cello.

articles.text: Tom Hanks and Helena Zengel in News of the World News of the World is an extraordinary, neo-western, adapted from the Paulette Jules 2016 novel. It is set in Texas in 1870, three years after the end of the Civil War. Confederate veteran Captain Jefferson Kyle Kidd (Tom Hanks), once a printer, now makes his improbable living by travelling from Texas town to Texas town reading the news, stories gleaned from newspapers from both near and far, standing stage center in candle-lit rooms, saying, “I read the news to anyone with ten cents and the time to hear it.” His audience is comprised of rough-hewn settlers, many still coming to terms with the defeat of the South. Many of those standing before him either can’t read, or spend every waking hour in physical labor; yet, all remain eager to hear the news of the world. As we soon come to realize, Captain Kidd is not only a respected man of letters, but also a storyteller and entertainer, and an enthusiastic, at times jocular reader of what could simply be the dry words on a page of newsprint. His mission is not only to inform but to capture the imaginations of his audience. On a trip to another town he discovers an overturned wagon on the side of the road. Investigating, he sees the body of a black freedman, hanging from a tree. Hiding nearby, among the brush, he spots a terrified young white girl (Helena Zengel), 12, dressed in Native American clothes, her blond hair bluntly cut. She is able to speak only Kiowa. He discovers some identifying papers in the wagon that say that she is German, her name is Johanna (she later explains that she is called Cicada), and she was abducted as a youngster and her parents killed. articles.text: After watching A Bag of Marbles (reviewed in the April 30th edition), what came to mind was that the Holocaust (also referred to as the Shoah), has been the subject of countless narrative films as well as a canon of what is described as Holocaust literature. Some works still use the Shoah only as a general referent or as a context (The Pianist, White Bird, The Boy in the Striped Pajamas, Sarah’s Key). And then there are films that portray the reality of the Holocaust in the starkest, most cruel and unrelenting detail, displaying am absence of humanity that is still impossible to comprehend. Though I had viewed director Steven Spielberg’s film Schindler’s List when it was first released and nominated for 12 Oscars in 1993, I recently watched it on Prime and found it still to be extraordinary. It is a work of art that transcends mere storytelling. It is profoundly evocative, at times grimly compelling, while implicitly asking countless questions regarding how and why the Holocaust could ever have taken place? Of course, it isn’t the intent of a narrative film such as Spielberg’s, adapted from the 1982 prize-wining book by Thomas Keneally, to offer answers; rather, its intent is to show through characters and dialogue and settings/imagery the all of it, Liam Neeson and Ben Kingsley in Schindler’s List

articles.text: The family friendly My Dog Skip, is a captivating story that focuses on the touching relationship between a 9-year-old boy, Willie Morris (Frankie Muniz), and his dog, a spunky Jack Russell Terrier that Willie names Skip. The film is set in Yazoo, Mississippi. The year is 1942. Willie, small for his age, is a lonely kid, often bullied by his larger classmates, especially a tough trio who take every opportunity to give him a hard time. He also has a standoffish relationship with his dad, Jack (Kevin Bacon), a gruff man, even bitter, who lost a leg in the Spanish Civil war. But it is his mom, Ellen (Diane Lane), who does her best to make Willie happy and often suggests to Jack that a dog would be the perfect companion for their isolated son. Willie of course agrees, pleads for a dog, but Jack firmly resists. Willie is about to have a birthday, even sends out invitation to his classmates, but on the day of the scheduled party only his grandparents show up, and his grandmother gives him a bowtie. But unbeknownst to Jack, Ellen brings to the party a small box and inside is a sweet little terrier pup, which delights Willie, and angers Jack. But Ellen prevails. And Willie and the pooch, soon named Skip, form an immediate bond and are soon inseparable. To Willie’s delight, kids who ignored him now pay attention to Skip, especially a classmate named Rivers Applewhite (Caitlin Wachs), a cute classmate that Willie thinks is special. There are, of course, subplots. One involves thuggish moonshiners who use an abandoned burial vault in the local cemetery to hide their illegal hooch. And there’s the bullying trio who dare Willie to stay all night among the tombstones while telling him that he should be on the look out for a witch who wanders about. There is even an awful moment when Willie, frustrated with his awkward and error-filled performance on the baseball field, gives Skip a hard swat on his nose with his baseball glove. As a result, the dog runs away. Filled with remorse, Willie begins a desperate search for Skip that ultimately involves the moonshiners. My Dog Skip, based on the memoir written by Willie Morris, a noted author and editor, unfailingly finds the sweet spot in this boy/dog narrative, demonstrating that our childhood memories, however dim, remain with us. My Dog Skip is a wonderful example. My Dog Skip. Directed by Jay Russell. Starring Frankie Muniz, Diane Lane, Kevin Bacon. 1 hr., 30 min. Rated PG. Released in 2000. articles.text: Hailee Steinfeld and Hayden Szeto in The Edge of Seventeen To capture the essence of being an adolescent, or as one critic called it, “The unbearable lightness of being a teenager,” is no easy thing. But The Edge of Seventeen, written and directed by Kelly Freemon Craig, is a coming-of-age story that is pitch perfect and gets it just right. The narrative stars Hailee Steinfeld portraying Nadine Byrd, 17, a junior in high school, whose bursting emotions swing from sweet to awkward to mean, while comprising a period in her life that can be intensely moving, disturbing, and funny. The film is set in Yazoo, Mississippi. The year is 1942. Willie, small for his age, is a lonely kid, often bullied by his larger classmates, especially a tough trio who take every opportunity to give him a hard time. He also has a standoffish relationship with his dad, Jack (Kevin Bacon), a gruff man, even bitter, who lost a leg in the Spanish Civil war. But it is his mom, Ellen (Diane Lane), who does her best to make Willie happy and often suggests to Jack that a dog would be the perfect companion for their isolated son. Willie of course agrees, pleads for a dog, but Jack firmly resists. Willie is about to have a birthday, even sends out invitation to his classmates, but on the day of the scheduled party only his grandparents show up, and his grandmother gives him a bowtie. But unbeknownst to Jack, Ellen brings to the party a small box and inside is a sweet little terrier pup, which delights Willie, and angers Jack. But Ellen prevails. And Willie and the pooch, soon named Skip, form an immediate bond and are soon inseparable. To Willie’s delight, kids who ignored him now pay attention to Skip, especially a classmate named Rivers Applewhite (Caitlin Wachs), a cute classmate that Willie thinks is special. There are, of course, subplots. One involves thuggish moonshiners who use an abandoned burial vault in the local cemetery to hide their illegal hooch. And there’s the bullying trio who dare Willie to stay all night among the tombstones while telling him that he should be on the look out for a witch who wanders about. There is even an awful moment when Willie, frustrated with his awkward and error-filled performance on the baseball field, gives Skip a hard swat on his nose with his baseball glove. As a result, the dog runs away. Filled with remorse, Willie begins a desperate search for Skip that ultimately involves the moonshiners. My Dog Skip, based on the memoir written by Willie Morris, a noted author and editor, unfailingly finds the sweet spot in this boy/dog narrative, demonstrating that our childhood memories, however dim, remain with us. articles.text: The True Story of Tamara De Lempicka & the Art of Survival is a visually stunning and sweeping feature documentary that traces the life and survival of the renowned painter through her powerful paintings – from her rise to international stardom in 1920s Paris, to her move to the United States in 1940, fleeing the rise of fascism, and her revival in the current art market. Tamara de Lempicka was the preeminent Art Deco painter, known for her high-gloss sensual nudes and portraits of high society during the Jazz Age. She was marginalized and gained notoriety for her romantic liaisons with her models and her indulgent, decadent lifestyle, but she was much more. The writer, director and producer of the film is Julie Rubio. She is a dynamic storyteller and is passionate about bringing to light the narratives of those often overlooked. As the president of Women in Film SF Bay Area, Rubio dedicates herself to empowering and elevating women in the film industry, fostering a supportive community for female filmmakers. Her most notable work, the critically acclaimed East Side Sushi, won accolades at 16 film festivals and garnered nominations for Cinema Tropical’s 2016 Best Latino Film of the Year and Mexico’s Diosa de Plata award for Best Picture. East Side Sushi, filmed in the Bay Area, is a compelling narrative of a single Latina mother’s pursuit of a better life and achieved widespread distribution through Samuel Goldwyn Company, Sony Home, HBO North America, and Netflix, where it became a trendsetter in popular and drama categories. Rubio’s latest movie, The True Story of Tamra De Lempicka & the Art of Survival will be shown at the Grand Lake Theater this weekend for three days only: • Saturday, May 17, 12 noon • Sunday, May 18, 12 noon • Monday, May 19, 4:15, 6:45, & 8:55 pm Purchase tickets online at Grand Lake Theater (https:// www.renaissancerialto.com/ Tamara.php)

pages.text: Wednesday, May 14, 2025 25 Features Walking on Wednesday Wednesday Walkers smell the roses By Dick Carter The Walking on Wednesdays group headed to the Morcom Rose Garden a few days in advance of Mother’s Day for the group’s annual visit. The group crossed Grand Avenue and went up Jean Street to the garden where its history was shared. A number of animal offers were received. Golden Gate Park offered elk and buffalo. F. M. “Borax” Smith offered a number of llamas from his large herd on his East Oakland estate, but the park directors decided not to have animals. Linda Vista Park’s conversion to a rose garden was a project of the Oakland Businessmen’s Garden Club in 1930 with the support of the City. It was originally known as the Municipal Rose Garden. Work began on the garden in 1931 and the first rose was planted on January 27, 1933. The garden opened officially on May 28, 1933, and work was completed in 1935 with Depression era funding. The park’s name was changed in 1954 to honor former Oakland Mayor Fred Morcom, who served from 1931 to 1933. The park has been refurbished at least twice, in the 1950s and 1990s, with many of the old roses, some going back to the 19th century, regrafted on new rootstock. There is a “No Dogs Allowed” sign at the park entrance, but on last year’s walk a park staff person told the walkers that dogs on leaches were okay. So, Jack Fischrup’s K-9 best friend Kojak also went in with the walkers to see the roses. The group stopped at the central reflecting pool and cascade steps where more information was shared. The garden’s design was inspired by gardens in Italy. The park has over 2,400 rose bushes in three areas. There are winding walkways with a reflecting pool across from a 14-step cascade that goes down the hillside to the west and an octagonal wedding terrace above with more rose beds. The essential design has changed little in the park’s nearly 90-year history. However, in the early 2000s, Oakland city workers’ hours to maintain the garden were reduced. A group of volunteers, the “Dedicated Deadheaders,” was organized to help keep the garden beautiful. They work every Wednesday and Saturday. Christian Boyle of the Oakland Department of Public Works is in charge of the garden, and he provided additional information about its history. Christian said wild turkeys are less frequent than in the past, but geese tried to make the garden a home. Their droppings made them unwelcome and he scared them off. Deer are a challenge, too. They have visited the garden and nipped buds, which explained some bushes’ lack of flowers. Wild onions are a problem too. The garden does not use chemicals, and this provides a “healthy garden,” but weeds are an issue. A study is currently being conducted by Merritt College students on weed suppression techniques. In the early 2000s “The Mothers’ Walk” was created above the reflecting pool to a Florentine oval garden at the north end of the park. There are brass plaques in the cement with the names of women honored each year in an annual Mother’s Day ceremony. The walkers appreciated Christian’s friendly, impromptu presentation and asked him to be part of their group photo at the cascade steps. Then the walkers splintered off on the paths to see different sections of the garden. The beds of roses on Mother’s Walk were especially beautiful. The group took their time and then retraced their route back to the Exedra at their own pace. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. articles.text: More than 100 guests gathered at George Mark Children’s House, a pediatric hospice in San Leandro, on May 2 for an unforgettable afternoon with beloved Star Wars characters. The special occasion brought Star Wars magic to children facing serious medical conditions. Now in its fourth year, Star Wars Day has become a cherished tradition for the George Mark community. This year’s celebration featured a special collaboration with Rancho Obi-Wan (ranchoobiwan. org), home to the world’s largest privately owned Star Wars memorabilia collection. In honor of the 20th anniversary of the movie Revenge of the Sith, Rancho ObiA patient has fun with Star Wars droids R2-D2 and Chopper. Wan curated a themed display of collectibles, toys, and promotional items. “For us, Rancho Obi-Wan has always been about helping to build a sense of community among fans of all ages,” said Ann Neumann, its president. “We help spread the fun and inspiration that Star Wars provides.” “We hope we brought some joy to George Mark Children’s House and helped create memories the families will hold close by sharing the love of a galaxy far, far away,” said founder Steve Sansweet. “It’s hard to put into words what it means to see the joy this day brings to our families,” said Shekinah Eliassen, CEO of George Mark Children’s House. “The Force was strong, but even stronger was the sense of community and love.” The celebration also included visits from Darth Vader, Chewbacca, General Leia, Stormtroopers, and fan-favorite droids R2-D2 and Chopper — thanks to volunteers from the Golden Gate Garrison of the 501st Legion, the Endor Base of the Rebel Legion, and the Bay Area Droid Builders. Guests enjoyed terrarium-making, caricatures, crafts, and toy giveaways, supported by Rancho Obi-Wan and Starlight Children’s Foundation. “Our mission is to provide the best quality of life for children with serious medical conditions,” said Kyle Amsler, Child Life Specialist at George Mark. “A day like this is all about joy – giving families a chance to create extraordinary memories together.” For many the experience was deeply emotional. “One mom came up to me with tears in her eyes and just said thank you,” said Events Coordinator Ricky Resurreccion. “She told me how much it meant to see her daughter so happy and to have a day that felt magical. Moments like that remind us why creating these kinds of experiences matter. articles.text: Piedmont kids and families brought their bikes to the first ever Gear Up Bike Festival last Saturday, May 10, from noon to 4:00 p.m. at the Havens School The festival provided information on bike maintenance and safety, as well as a bike swap that gave away five helmets and eight bikes to members of the community. Over 100 attendees visited the inaugural event, which began with a family biking workshop by Bike East Bay. The event also featured a Mister Softee ice cream truck, a bike obstacle course by the Piedmont Police Department and Piedmont Scouts, pedal-powered blender smoothies by Piedmont Scouts, and pedal-powered spin art by inventor group Rock the Bike. Visitors were also able to test ride E-bikes from electric bike shop The New Wheel. Oakland Trek ran a bike maintenance table at the event to help and inform attending cyclists, and an additional class teaching kids how to be safe on bikes. The event’s bike swap gave kids and adults a way to bring outgrown bikes, equipment, and parts to swap with other families. As part of the bike swap, the event gave away five helmets and eight bikes, donated from listings on Buy Nothing facebook groups. Bike to Work Day The event was organized by Piedmont parent Daniel Sherman as a way to help publicize the upcoming Bike to Work Day on May 15. The Bay Area biking event encourages people to bike to work, school, or anywhere they need to go. “When you bike, you’re connected to your environment and the people around you,” said Sherman. “You’re aware of what’s going on, and you’re not going from one box (your house) to the next box (your car) to the next box (your classroom). Instead you’re interacting with people, you’re paying attention, it gives kids autonomy, independence and pride.” Sherman and his family enjoy cycling to get around and encourages others to try it as well. “The Gear Up event was great, but look forward to May 15,” said Sherman. Pedaling the bike turns a wheel, and kids pour in paint to create patterns. Two children maneuver through an obstacle course at the Gear Up Bike Festival. The pedal-powered spin art hangs to dry. Oakland Trek offered bike repair and maintenance advice at their table. Piedmont Scouts gave out pedal-powered smoothies from a bicyclepowered blender. An array of bikes were contributed to the bike swap to help kids get into cycling for free.

Shindler’s List has at its center German industrialist Oskar Schindler (Liam Neeson), initially portrayed as a war profiteer. Arriving in Krakow, Poland in 1939, he joins the Nazi Party and lavishly cultivates high-ranking officers who will help him to find captive Jewish labor needed for his factory. It is only when he witnesses the mass killing of the Jews forced to live in the Krakow Ghetto that he comes to comprehend the true meaning of what was abstractly referred to as “the final solution.” Schindler’s journey from that moment is both transformative and horrifying. They really are. I always get the feeling when I get an award - my initial response is, you know, I’m just doing my job to the best of my ability,” said Bowers. Bowers moved to Piedmont in search of a healthy and meaningful work-life balance. With good schools for his children and a community that emphasizes volunteering, Piedmont was “just too good of an opportunity to pass up” for Bowers and his family. At times, his kids were able to drop by to enjoy lunch together with him in his office. “I’ve really grown to really appreciate being here for the past eleven years,” said Bowers. “It’s been meaningful professionally, and it’s been meaningful from a personal standpoint.” Bowers joined the Piedmont Police Department as a Captain in 2014 after 18 years of work with the San Jose Police Department. Nine years ago he succeeded his mentor, Chief Rikki Goede, with whom he worked in San Jose. Bowers has served as Police Chief through times of great social change, including the Covid-19 pandemic. “It’s been an honor and a privilege to be the Piedmont Police Chief,” said Bowers. “To the Piedmont community, I say thank you, it’s been a good ride. I’ll still see folks around town as my youngest finishes high school, but I’m really excited about the future of this organization and the future of this city.” Humble by nature, Bowers models the ideal attitude for a public servant and leader in the community, and his character and kind perspective should be prime examples for this year’s parade theme: “Traditions Thrive in 2025.” Big Climb Continued from page 1 “It was just super touching to see Russell on FaceTime and then have his wife and his two boys there,” said McNulty. “For them to see the impact that that organization has had on research and care and the survivor stories for them to hear, I think that was really reassuring and helpful,” said McNulty.
